title: Plotly Express Cheatsheet
name: Plotly Express Cheatsheet
description: High-density syntax recall for plotly.express (plotly.py 6.8.0), focused on rapid figure generation, Cartesian and statistical charts, 3D/geographic plots, faceting, and animations.

entries.title: Initialize Plotly Express defaults
entries.problem: Set global figure defaults for a project.
entries.trigger: When starting a notebook, script, or service that creates many figures.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import plotly.io as pio

px.defaults.template = "plotly_white"
px.defaults.width = 900
px.defaults.height = 540
pio.renderers.default = "notebook"
fig = px.scatter(px.data.iris(), x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Set defaults once per process. Use a shared template for consistency.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting the renderer in headless or notebook environments.

entries.title: Create a figure from a pandas DataFrame
entries.problem: Build a chart from tidy tabular data.
entries.trigger: When your input is a DataFrame with one row per observation.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter(df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: DataFrame columns map directly to arguments. This is the default workflow.
entries.common_bug: Passing column names without a DataFrame.

entries.title: Use array-like inputs without a DataFrame
entries.problem: Plot quick data without constructing a DataFrame first.
entries.trigger: When values already exist as lists, numpy arrays, or Series.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import numpy as np

x = np.arange(10)
y = np.array([1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100])
fig = px.line(x=x, y=y, title="Array input")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Array-like inputs are converted internally. A DataFrame is still better for multi-encoding workflows.
entries.common_bug: Expecting column-name behavior without providing a DataFrame.

entries.title: Use wide-format data
entries.problem: Plot multiple series from wide columns.
entries.trigger: When each metric already lives in its own column.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": np.arange(6), "a": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], "b": [2, 4, 1, 6, 5, 7] })
fig = px.line(df, x="x", y=["a", "b"], title="Wide format line")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Passing a list to x or y switches the figure into wide mode. Keep series names meaningful.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that wide mode changes the legend and trace splitting behavior.

entries.title: Use tidy long-form data
entries.problem: Plot the same measure across categories in one column.
entries.trigger: When your data is already normalized into variable/value columns.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.bar(df, x="day", y="total_bill", color="sex", title="Long-form bar")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Long-form is the safest default for px. It scales well to faceting and animation.
entries.common_bug: Trying to encode multiple wide columns when the data is already long.

entries.title: Create a customized scatter plot
entries.problem: Show relationships with color, size, hover fields, and labels.
entries.trigger: When exploring two continuous variables with extra encodings.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter(
    df,
    x="sepal_width",
    y="sepal_length",
    color="species",
    size="petal_length",
    hover_name="species",
    hover_data=["petal_width"],
    title="Customized scatter"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Scatter is the most common px entry point. Use hover_data for extra context.
entries.common_bug: Over-encoding too many variables and making the plot unreadable.

entries.title: Create a large scatter plot with WebGL
entries.problem: Keep point rendering responsive for large datasets.
entries.trigger: When plotting thousands of markers.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": np.random.randn(50000), "y": np.random.randn(50000)})
fig = px.scatter(df, x="x", y="y", render_mode="webgl", opacity=0.55, title="WebGL scatter")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use webgl for large point counts. It improves interactivity but reduces pure vector output.
entries.common_bug: Assuming WebGL solves every performance issue in very large figures.

entries.title: Create a line chart
entries.problem: Show ordered values over time or another continuous axis.
entries.trigger: When one dimension must be connected in sequence.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("country == 'Canada'")
fig = px.line(df, x="year", y="lifeExp", title="Canada life expectancy")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: line supports wide and long data. Use markers only when you need discrete points visible.
entries.common_bug: Using line charts for unordered categories.

entries.title: Create a line chart with markers
entries.problem: Show trends while keeping individual observations visible.
entries.trigger: When each sampled point matters.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("country == 'Canada'")
fig = px.line(df, x="year", y="lifeExp", markers=True, title="Line with markers")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: markers=True adds visible vertices. Useful for sparse time series.
entries.common_bug: Turning on markers for dense series and cluttering the plot.

entries.title: Create an area chart
entries.problem: Show cumulative or filled time-series style data.
entries.trigger: When filled lines communicate magnitude better than plain lines.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("continent == 'Asia' and year >= 1970")
fig = px.area(df, x="year", y="pop", color="country", title="Area chart")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Area is a filled line workflow. Use with care when multiple series overlap.
entries.common_bug: Stacking many filled series without checking legend order.

entries.title: Create a grouped bar chart
entries.problem: Compare category totals side by side.
entries.trigger: When summarizing categorical metrics across groups.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.bar(df, x="day", y="total_bill", color="sex", barmode="group", title="Grouped bars")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use color plus barmode='group' for side-by-side comparison. This is a standard reporting chart.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to aggregate when raw rows should be summarized first.

entries.title: Create a stacked bar chart
entries.problem: Show part-to-whole composition within each category.
entries.trigger: When the total and its components both matter.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.bar(df, x="day", y="total_bill", color="sex", barmode="stack", title="Stacked bars")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Stacking works best when categories are few. Use category_orders to control order.
entries.common_bug: Stacking too many categories and hiding differences.

entries.title: Create a horizontal bar chart
entries.problem: Improve readability for long category labels.
entries.trigger: When category names are too long for vertical bars.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips().groupby("day", as_index=False)["total_bill"].sum()
fig = px.bar(df, x="total_bill", y="day", orientation="h", title="Horizontal bars")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: orientation='h' flips the axes. This is useful for ranked lists.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to swap x and y when changing orientation.

entries.title: Create a bar chart with labels
entries.problem: Show values directly on bars.
entries.trigger: When the chart will be read without tooltips.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips().groupby("day", as_index=False)["total_bill"].sum()
fig = px.bar(df, x="day", y="total_bill", text_auto=True, title="Bars with labels")
fig.update_traces(textposition="outside")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: text_auto is a fast way to add readable labels. Use it for summary charts.
entries.common_bug: Labels collide on small figures without enough margin.

entries.title: Create a funnel chart
entries.problem: Show stage-by-stage drop-off.
entries.trigger: When modeling pipelines, conversions, or process steps.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"stage": ["Visit", "Sign up", "Trial", "Purchase"], "count": [100, 60, 40, 20]})
fig = px.funnel(df, x="count", y="stage", title="Funnel")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Funnel uses ordered stages. It is best for linear progression.
entries.common_bug: Reordering stages incorrectly and changing the meaning.

entries.title: Create a funnel area chart
entries.problem: Compare funnel stages with area emphasis.
entries.trigger: When visual emphasis should widen or narrow by stage value.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"stage": ["Visit", "Sign up", "Trial", "Purchase"], "count": [100, 60, 40, 20]})
fig = px.funnel_area(df, names="stage", values="count", title="Funnel area")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: funnel_area is useful for compact stage comparison. Keep stage count small.
entries.common_bug: Treating funnel area as an exact quantitative chart.

entries.title: Create a timeline chart
entries.problem: Show task durations with start and end dates.
entries.trigger: When visualizing schedules or project timelines.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame([
    {"task": "Design", "start": "2026-01-01", "finish": "2026-01-20"},
    {"task": "Build", "start": "2026-01-15", "finish": "2026-02-28"},
    {"task": "Launch", "start": "2026-03-01", "finish": "2026-03-10"},
])
fig = px.timeline(df, x_start="start", x_end="finish", y="task", title="Project timeline")
fig.update_yaxes(autorange="reversed")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use x_start and x_end. Reverse the y-axis for conventional Gantt ordering.
entries.common_bug: Leaving date strings unparsed when the input is inconsistent.

entries.title: Create a scatter plot with error bars
entries.problem: Show uncertainty or measurement variation.
entries.trigger: When values have known error ranges.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [2.2, 2.8, 3.6], "err": [0.2, 0.3, 0.15]})
fig = px.scatter(df, x="x", y="y", error_y="err", title="Scatter with error bars")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use error_x and error_y for uncertainty ranges. Symmetric bars are the default.
entries.common_bug: Mixing absolute and relative error values without documenting the units.

entries.title: Create a line chart with asymmetric error bars
entries.problem: Show separate positive and negative uncertainty.
entries.trigger: When lower and upper confidence bounds differ.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "x": [1, 2, 3],
    "y": [2.0, 3.0, 2.5],
    "plus": [1.0, 0.8, 1.2],
    "minus": [0.5, 0.6, 0.4],
})
fig = px.line(df, x="x", y="y", error_y="plus", error_y_minus="minus", title="Asymmetric error bars")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use *_minus columns for asymmetric bars. This is the cleanest px interface for bounds.
entries.common_bug: Reversing positive and negative error columns.

entries.title: Create a histogram
entries.problem: Show the distribution of a single numeric variable.
entries.trigger: When you need frequency counts or binning.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.histogram(df, x="total_bill", nbins=30, title="Histogram")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Histogram is the default distribution chart. Adjust bins for readability.
entries.common_bug: Comparing raw distributions without normalizing or grouping when needed.

entries.title: Create a normalized histogram
entries.problem: Compare distributions by percentage instead of counts.
entries.trigger: When groups have different sample sizes.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.histogram(df, x="total_bill", color="sex", histnorm="percent", barmode="overlay", opacity=0.6, title="Percent histogram")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: histnorm controls the y-axis meaning. Overlay plus opacity is common for comparisons.
entries.common_bug: Reading normalized histograms as if they were raw counts.

entries.title: Create a histogram with marginal rug
entries.problem: Add raw-value context to a distribution plot.
entries.trigger: When you want the histogram plus data density hints.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.histogram(df, x="total_bill", marginal="rug", title="Histogram with rug")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Marginal plots are compact and useful for quick diagnostics. Rug shows individual samples.
entries.common_bug: Using too many marginal layers and cluttering the view.

entries.title: Create a box plot
entries.problem: Compare quartiles and outliers across categories.
entries.trigger: When summarizing distribution shape.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.box(df, x="day", y="total_bill", color="sex", title="Box plot")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Box plots are efficient for group comparisons. Use category_orders for stable ordering.
entries.common_bug: Interpreting sparse categories as statistically meaningful.

entries.title: Create a violin plot with points
entries.problem: Show distribution shape plus raw samples.
entries.trigger: When you want a richer view than a box plot.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.violin(df, x="day", y="total_bill", box=True, points="all", color="sex", title="Violin plot")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: box=True and points="all" are the common production combination. Use opacity carefully.
entries.common_bug: Overplotting too many raw points on large datasets.

entries.title: Create a strip plot
entries.problem: Show individual observations without aggregation.
entries.trigger: When each row is important and categories are few.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.strip(df, x="day", y="total_bill", color="sex", title="Strip plot")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Strip plots are useful for small-to-medium samples. They complement box and violin charts.
entries.common_bug: Using strip plots on very large datasets without jitter control.

entries.title: Create an ECDF plot
entries.problem: Show cumulative distribution without binning.
entries.trigger: When comparing percentiles or distribution dominance.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.ecdf(df, x="total_bill", color="sex", title="ECDF")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: ECDF is a good alternative to histograms for precise cumulative comparison. It preserves sample ordering.
entries.common_bug: Using ECDF when the audience expects frequency bins.

entries.title: Create a density heatmap
entries.problem: Show 2D concentration for large scatter clouds.
entries.trigger: When scatter points overlap heavily.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.density_heatmap(df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", nbinsx=40, nbinsy=40, title="Density heatmap")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Density heatmap bins points into a grid. It is useful for crowded relationships.
entries.common_bug: Choosing bins too coarse or too fine for the data scale.

entries.title: Create a density contour plot
entries.problem: Show isolines of concentration in 2D.
entries.trigger: When you need density structure instead of filled bins.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.density_contour(df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species", title="Density contour")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Density contours are useful for smooth cluster structure. Pair with scatter only when necessary.
entries.common_bug: Overlaying too many contours and making the figure hard to parse.

entries.title: Create a pie chart
entries.problem: Show simple part-to-whole composition.
entries.trigger: When there are few categories and totals matter.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips().groupby("day", as_index=False)["total_bill"].sum()
fig = px.pie(df, names="day", values="total_bill", title="Pie chart")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Pie charts should stay simple. Use only for small category counts.
entries.common_bug: Using pie charts with many slices or similar values.

entries.title: Create a donut chart
entries.problem: Show part-to-whole with center space.
entries.trigger: When a pie chart needs a label area or visual emphasis.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips().groupby("day", as_index=False)["total_bill"].sum()
fig = px.pie(df, names="day", values="total_bill", hole=0.4, title="Donut chart")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: hole creates the donut shape. Keep labels concise.
entries.common_bug: Treating donut holes as extra data space instead of decoration.

entries.title: Create a sunburst chart
entries.problem: Show hierarchical totals in radial form.
entries.trigger: When you need nested categories with parent-child structure.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips().groupby(["day", "sex"], as_index=False)["total_bill"].sum()
fig = px.sunburst(df, path=["day", "sex"], values="total_bill", title="Sunburst")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use path for hierarchy. Values control sector size.
entries.common_bug: Mixing incompatible hierarchy columns or missing parents.

entries.title: Create a treemap
entries.problem: Show hierarchical composition in nested rectangles.
entries.trigger: When the hierarchy is deep and labels must remain compact.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips().groupby(["day", "sex"], as_index=False)["total_bill"].sum()
fig = px.treemap(df, path=["day", "sex"], values="total_bill", title="Treemap")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Treemaps are compact hierarchical summaries. They are usually denser than sunburst charts.
entries.common_bug: Using treemaps for precise comparison of many similar values.

entries.title: Create an icicle chart
entries.problem: Show hierarchy with top-down rectangular levels.
entries.trigger: When hierarchy depth is important and a top-down layout helps.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips().groupby(["day", "sex"], as_index=False)["total_bill"].sum()
fig = px.icicle(df, path=["day", "sex"], values="total_bill", title="Icicle")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Icicles are useful for clear level separation. Use them for tree-like breakdowns.
entries.common_bug: Supplying an unbalanced hierarchy and expecting equal visual depth.

entries.title: Create a scatter matrix
entries.problem: Inspect pairwise relationships across several numeric variables.
entries.trigger: When you need a quick multivariate overview.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter_matrix(
    df,
    dimensions=["sepal_length", "sepal_width", "petal_length", "petal_width"],
    color="species",
    title="Scatter matrix"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Limit dimensions to a small set of useful columns. SPLOMs get crowded fast.
entries.common_bug: Using too many dimensions and losing readability.

entries.title: Create parallel coordinates
entries.problem: Compare many continuous variables per row.
entries.trigger: When you need a compact multivariate line view.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.parallel_coordinates(df, color="sepal_length", title="Parallel coordinates")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Color can be numeric for continuous encoding. This is useful for feature comparison.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that many rows can make the lines unreadable.

entries.title: Create parallel categories
entries.problem: Show categorical relationships across multiple dimensions.
entries.trigger: When comparing category flows or attribute combinations.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.parallel_categories(df, dimensions=["day", "time", "sex", "smoker"], title="Parallel categories")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: This is the categorical companion to parallel coordinates. Keep dimensions small.
entries.common_bug: Adding too many categories and creating spaghetti-like flows.

entries.title: Create a 3D scatter plot
entries.problem: Show three numeric dimensions and category color together.
entries.trigger: When 3D structure matters more than flat projections.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter_3d(df, x="sepal_length", y="sepal_width", z="petal_length", color="species", title="3D scatter")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: 3D plots are interactive and rotate in browser. Use them selectively.
entries.common_bug: Overusing 3D when 2D plus facets would be clearer.

entries.title: Create a 3D line plot
entries.problem: Plot a path through 3D space.
entries.trigger: When trajectory or path geometry must be shown.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

t = np.linspace(0, 12, 200)
df = pd.DataFrame({"x": np.cos(t), "y": np.sin(t), "z": t})
fig = px.line_3d(df, x="x", y="y", z="z", title="3D line")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: line_3d is useful for trajectories and parametric curves. Keep paths smooth and sparse enough to inspect.
entries.common_bug: Expecting 3D lines to export as clean vectors in every backend.

entries.title: Create a polar scatter plot
entries.problem: Plot radius and angle data.
entries.trigger: When working with circular measurements or directional data.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"r": np.random.rand(30), "theta": np.linspace(0, 360, 30), "group": ["A"]*15 + ["B"]*15})
fig = px.scatter_polar(df, r="r", theta="theta", color="group", title="Polar scatter")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Polar plots need angle conventions to be clear. Label the domain explicitly.
entries.common_bug: Confusing degrees and radians in theta values.

entries.title: Create a polar line chart
entries.problem: Show radial sequences connected by angle.
entries.trigger: When polar observations are ordered along a circle.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.DataFrame({"r": np.random.rand(20), "theta": np.linspace(0, 360, 20)})
fig = px.line_polar(df, r="r", theta="theta", line_close=True, title="Polar line")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: line_close closes the polygon when needed. It is useful for cyclical profiles.
entries.common_bug: Leaving a cyclic series open when the first and last points should connect.

entries.title: Create a polar bar chart
entries.problem: Show category magnitudes on a circular axis.
entries.trigger: When a radial bar layout is useful for directional summaries.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"theta": ["N", "E", "S", "W"], "r": [1, 2, 3, 4]})
fig = px.bar_polar(df, r="r", theta="theta", title="Polar bars")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Polar bars are compact but should remain simple. They work best with a few categories.
entries.common_bug: Using too many bars and making angle comparisons difficult.

entries.title: Create a ternary scatter plot
entries.problem: Plot compositional data with three parts summing to a whole.
entries.trigger: When every point is a three-part mixture.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [0.2, 0.4, 0.3], "b": [0.5, 0.2, 0.4], "c": [0.3, 0.4, 0.3], "grp": ["X", "Y", "Z"]})
fig = px.scatter_ternary(df, a="a", b="b", c="c", color="grp", title="Ternary scatter")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Ternary plots require compositional interpretation. Ensure values are normalized consistently.
entries.common_bug: Feeding non-compositional values without normalization.

entries.title: Create a ternary line plot
entries.problem: Show a connected path through ternary space.
entries.trigger: When mixtures evolve over ordered steps.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2], "b": [0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.5], "c": [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.3]})
fig = px.line_ternary(df, a="a", b="b", c="c", title="Ternary line")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Ternary lines are useful for trajectories in composition space. Keep the sequence ordered.
entries.common_bug: Unsorted rows causing a misleading path.

entries.title: Create a geographic scatter plot
entries.problem: Plot points on a global map without tiles.
entries.trigger: When lat/lon coordinates are available.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("year == 2007")
fig = px.scatter_geo(df, lat="lat", lon="lon", color="continent", hover_name="country", size="pop", title="Geo scatter")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: scatter_geo is the stable non-Mapbox geo workflow. Good for world-scale maps.
entries.common_bug: Supplying coordinates with the wrong latitude/longitude columns.

entries.title: Create a choropleth map
entries.problem: Color regions by a numeric metric.
entries.trigger: When each geometry has a matching code or name.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("year == 2007")
fig = px.choropleth(df, locations="iso_alpha", color="lifeExp", hover_name="country", color_continuous_scale="Viridis", title="Choropleth")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Choropleths require valid location codes or geojson. Use a continuous scale for numeric values.
entries.common_bug: Mismatching location identifiers with the geometry source.

entries.title: Create a density map
entries.problem: Visualize point density on a geographic map.
entries.trigger: When point concentration matters more than each point.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"lat": [23.8103, 23.7806, 23.7465], "lon": [90.4125, 90.2794, 90.3750], "value": [10, 20, 30]})
fig = px.density_map(df, lat="lat", lon="lon", z="value", radius=20, center=dict(lat=23.8103, lon=90.4125), zoom=9, title="Density map")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: density_map is the stable map density workflow. Keep point coordinates accurate.
entries.common_bug: Mixing up density_map with point scatter and expecting one marker per row.

entries.title: Create a map-style scatter plot
entries.problem: Plot geographic points on a tile-based map when needed.
entries.trigger: When you want map tiles and interactive pan/zoom.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.carshare()
fig = px.scatter_map(df, lat="centroid_lat", lon="centroid_lon", color="peak_hour", size="car_hours", title="Scatter map")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use the stable map API rather than older mapbox-specific examples where possible. Keep the map centered.
entries.common_bug: Using deprecated or legacy mapbox naming in new code.

entries.title: Create a choropleth map with modern mapping workflow
entries.problem: Render region shading on a map-style interface.
entries.trigger: When a tile-based or map-oriented choropleth is required.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("year == 2007")
fig = px.choropleth_map(df, geojson=None, locations="iso_alpha", color="lifeExp", title="Choropleth map")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use the modern map-oriented chart when the workflow requires map styling. Validate location fields carefully.
entries.common_bug: Assuming the same location encoding works across every choropleth variant.

entries.title: Create an animated scatter plot
entries.problem: Show how a relationship changes across time.
entries.trigger: When you need a frame-by-frame progression.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder()
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="gdpPercap", y="lifeExp",
    animation_frame="year", animation_group="country",
    size="pop", color="continent", hover_name="country",
    log_x=True, size_max=60, title="Animated scatter"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: animation_frame selects frames and animation_group preserves identity. This is the classic px animation pattern.
entries.common_bug: Leaving out animation_group and losing object constancy.

entries.title: Create an animated line chart
entries.problem: Animate a series over time.
entries.trigger: When each row or entity evolves frame-by-frame.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder()
fig = px.line(
    df, x="year", y="lifeExp",
    color="continent",
    animation_frame="year",
    animation_group="country",
    title="Animated line"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Animated line charts are best for small frame counts. Keep traces simple.
entries.common_bug: Combining too many groups with many frames and making playback sluggish.

entries.title: Create a faceted scatter plot
entries.problem: Split a scatter chart by category.
entries.trigger: When comparing the same relationship across groups.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.scatter(df, x="total_bill", y="tip", color="sex", facet_col="time", title="Faceted scatter")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Facets are ideal for side-by-side subgroup comparisons. Use consistent axes for easier reading.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that facets can shrink the plot and make labels tiny.

entries.title: Create a faceted histogram with wrap
entries.problem: Split a histogram across multiple panels with wrapping.
entries.trigger: When one categorical dimension has several levels.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.histogram(df, x="total_bill", facet_col="day", facet_col_wrap=2, color="sex", title="Wrapped facets")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: facet_col_wrap keeps layouts compact. This is useful for 3+ categories.
entries.common_bug: Setting too many facets per row and making each panel too small.

entries.title: Create a faceted box plot
entries.problem: Compare distributions across two grouping dimensions.
entries.trigger: When category interaction matters.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.box(df, x="day", y="total_bill", facet_col="time", color="sex", title="Faceted box plot")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Faceting plus box plots is a common statistical reporting pattern. Keep the number of categories moderate.
entries.common_bug: Using facets and too many hue levels at the same time.

entries.title: Create a faceted line chart
entries.problem: Compare time series across categories in separate panels.
entries.trigger: When overlapping lines become too dense.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("country in ['Canada', 'United States', 'Mexico']")
fig = px.line(df, x="year", y="lifeExp", color="country", facet_col="country", title="Faceted line chart")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Faceting often reads better than stacking many lines in one panel. Use identical axes for comparison.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting to share axes, which breaks comparison between panels.

entries.title: Control facet spacing
entries.problem: Tighten or loosen space between panels.
entries.trigger: When layout density needs adjustment.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.scatter(df, x="total_bill", y="tip", facet_col="day", facet_col_spacing=0.03, facet_row_spacing=0.03, title="Facet spacing")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Fine-tune spacing when panels feel too cramped. Spacing is in paper units.
entries.common_bug: Making spacing too small and causing label overlap.

entries.title: Apply discrete color sequencing
entries.problem: Use a consistent categorical palette.
entries.trigger: When category colors must remain stable across charts.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species",
    color_discrete_sequence=px.colors.qualitative.Dark24,
    title="Discrete palette"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use qualitative palettes for categories. Keep palette choice consistent across a project.
entries.common_bug: Using a continuous palette for categorical data.

entries.title: Apply continuous color scaling
entries.problem: Map numeric values to a gradient.
entries.trigger: When color represents a measurable quantity.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="petal_length",
    color_continuous_scale=px.colors.sequential.Viridis,
    title="Continuous color scale"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use sequential or diverging scales for numeric fields. Normalize ranges when comparing figures.
entries.common_bug: Using a diverging scale without a meaningful midpoint.

entries.title: Reorder categories explicitly
entries.problem: Enforce stable axis and legend order.
entries.trigger: When default category order is not acceptable.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.tips()
fig = px.bar(
    df, x="day", y="total_bill", color="sex",
    category_orders={"day": ["Thur", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"], "sex": ["Female", "Male"]},
    title="Ordered categories"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: category_orders controls axes, legends, and facets. Use it for reproducibility.
entries.common_bug: Assuming alphabetical order when data order changes by input source.

entries.title: Rename labels for publication output
entries.problem: Replace raw column names with presentation-friendly text.
entries.trigger: When the output will be shown to users or stakeholders.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species",
    labels={"sepal_width": "Sepal Width", "sepal_length": "Sepal Length", "species": "Species"},
    title="Renamed labels"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: labels updates axis titles, legend names, and hover labels. It is the cleanest naming control in px.
entries.common_bug: Leaving raw database column names in stakeholder-facing charts.

entries.title: Set title and subtitle
entries.problem: Add chart context without manual annotations.
entries.trigger: When the figure needs a report-ready heading.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter(
    df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species",
    title="Iris scatter",
    subtitle="Sepal width vs sepal length"
)
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: title and subtitle are first-class px arguments. Use them before custom layout annotations.
entries.common_bug: Overloading the title with too much explanatory text.

entries.title: Update layout after figure creation
entries.problem: Adjust margins, legends, and overall layout.
entries.trigger: When px defaults are close but not final.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter(df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species", title="Layout updates")
fig.update_layout(legend_title_text="Species", margin=dict(l=40, r=20, t=60, b=40))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: update_layout is the standard post-processing step. Keep figure construction separate from styling.
entries.common_bug: Applying layout edits before figure construction is complete.

entries.title: Update traces after figure creation
entries.problem: Standardize marker, line, or hover behavior across traces.
entries.trigger: When a chart needs final production polishing.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter(df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species", title="Trace updates")
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=10, opacity=0.8))
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: update_traces affects all traces unless filtered. Use it for common styling.
entries.common_bug: Accidentally changing every trace when only one should be modified.

entries.title: Update x-axes and y-axes
entries.problem: Format axes after a px chart is created.
entries.trigger: When axis titles, ticks, or ranges need final control.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.gapminder().query("country == 'Canada'")
fig = px.line(df, x="year", y="lifeExp", title="Axis formatting")
fig.update_xaxes(title="Year")
fig.update_yaxes(title="Life Expectancy", range=[50, 90])
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: Use axis-specific methods for final formatting. They are clearer than editing layout directly.
entries.common_bug: Setting a range that clips valid data points.

entries.title: Show a figure interactively
entries.problem: Render the chart in the current environment.
entries.trigger: When you want browser or notebook display.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

fig = px.scatter(px.data.iris(), x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: show() uses the current renderer. Choose the renderer once in project setup.
entries.common_bug: Expecting show() to persist as a file artifact.

entries.title: Write an interactive HTML file
entries.problem: Save a self-contained chart for sharing.
entries.trigger: When the output must be opened without Python.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

fig = px.scatter(px.data.iris(), x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species")
fig.write_html("iris_scatter.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")
entries.minimal_notes: HTML export is self-contained and easy to distribute. CDN mode reduces file size.
entries.common_bug: Forgetting that offline environments may not load CDN assets.

entries.title: Write a static image
entries.problem: Export a PNG for reports or slides.
entries.trigger: When a fixed-resolution artifact is needed.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

fig = px.scatter(px.data.iris(), x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", color="species")
fig.write_image("iris_scatter.png", scale=2)
entries.minimal_notes: Static image export requires a supported image engine such as kaleido. Use scale for resolution.
entries.common_bug: Running export in a container without the required image backend.

entries.title: Extract trendline results
entries.problem: Retrieve regression outputs from a trendline figure.
entries.trigger: When you need model statistics from an OLS fit.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

df = px.data.iris()
fig = px.scatter(df, x="sepal_width", y="sepal_length", trendline="ols")
results = px.get_trendline_results(fig)
print(results[["px_fit_results"]])
entries.minimal_notes: get_trendline_results is only meaningful for OLS trendlines. It returns statsmodels results objects.
entries.common_bug: Expecting this to work for non-OLS trendline types.

entries.title: Use px defaults for repeated styling
entries.problem: Standardize theme, size, and rendering across many figures.
entries.trigger: When a project repeatedly reuses the same chart style.
entries.snippet:
import plotly.express as px

px.defaults.template = "plotly_white"
px.defaults.width = 960
px.defaults.height = 540
fig = px.bar(px.data.tips(), x="day", y="total_bill", color="sex")
fig.show()
entries.minimal_notes: px.defaults reduces repeated boilerplate. It is ideal for team-wide chart consistency.
entries.common_bug: Mutating defaults deep in application code and creating inconsistent figures.

quick_references.title: Common px keyword arguments
rows: Encode a variable by marker symbol.
Encode a variable by marker size.

common_errors.error: Figure does not render in headless environment.
common_errors.cause: Default renderer requires a browser or GUI environment, which is missing in headless runners.
common_errors.solution: Explicitly configure a headless renderer (e.g., pio.renderers.default = 'json' or 'browser') or save directly to a file.

common_errors.cause: Passing column names to px functions that do not match the columns in the supplied DataFrame.
common_errors.solution: Verify column names in df.columns before plotting, or use array-like inputs directly without a DataFrame.

common_errors.error: Sluggish zoom/pan with thousands of data points.
common_errors.cause: Default SVG rendering mode struggles with high marker counts.
common_errors.solution: Set render_mode='webgl' in px.scatter or px.line to offload rendering to the GPU.

common_errors.error: Animation frames out of sequence or missing categories.
common_errors.cause: Data frame is not sorted by the animation frame key, causing random playback ordering.
common_errors.solution: Sort the DataFrame by the animation column (e.g., df.sort_values('year')) before creating the plot.

common_errors.error: Color sequence does not map consistently across plots.
common_errors.cause: Depending on default color ordering, which changes based on which categories appear first in the data.
common_errors.solution: Use category_orders to force a stable categorical order and layout mapping.

performance_checklist.recommendations: Use render_mode='webgl' for scatter charts with over 5,000 markers to prevent SVG rendering bottlenecks.
Drop unused columns and filter rows from DataFrames before passing them to Plotly Express to reduce serialization overhead.
Limit the number of active WebGL contexts on a single page to prevent browser crashes.
Use write_html with include_plotlyjs='cdn' to keep exported HTML files small (under 3MB instead of 6MB+).
Reduce animation frames and groups when creating interactive animations; pre-aggregate data where possible.

production_checklist: Verify figure sizes (width and height) explicitly rather than relying on browser window defaults.
Use category_orders to ensure categorical values appear in a deterministic, logical sequence.
Replace raw database/DataFrame column names with presentation-friendly text using the labels dictionary.
Check continuous color scales for colorblind accessibility and appropriate luminance range.
Configure the appropriate renderer or default template once at the entry point of the project.
Export high-resolution static images using scale>=2 to prevent blurriness in reports or slide decks.
Clean hover labels by using hover_name and hover_data to exclude raw keys that confuse stakeholders.
